name: Interpretive dance

narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

instructor.persona: A focused, expressive choreographer who emphasizes 'feeling the movement' over 'hitting the mark'.

This is Interpretive dance. Early 20th century to present.

Title card: Interpretive dance · United States; Europe · Early 20th century to present

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The movement began around 1900 with Isadora Duncan, who rebelled against the strictures of classical ballet.

Duncan and Ruth St. Denis are credited as the primary roots of the style, with later contributions from Martha Graham, Doris Humphrey, and Merce Cunningham, who each added psychological depth or avant-garde techniques to the form.
on_screen: Map: United States; Europe · Global
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dance serves as a medium for translating human emotions, conditions, or fantasies into movement.
It is used both as a performing art on concert stages and Broadway, and as a pedagogical tool for 'musical nurture' in early childhood education.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance prioritizes natural movement over technical virtuosity.
It frequently includes grandiloquent arm movements, turns, and drops to the floor.
Dancers often perform barefoot to facilitate a more grounded and fluid connection to the space.
Watch for Fall and Recovery, Floor Work.
on_screen: Hero video — MISSING
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Exploration of new or unconventional floor work and spatial paths.
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: While originally associated with classical concert music, interpretive dance does not strictly require music.
It can be performed to avant-garde compositions or in silence.
Listen for the Piano, Orchestral strings, Electronic/Avant-garde sounds.
The pulse is Variable.
The soundscape ranges from traditional classical concert music to avant-garde and chance-based compositions, or even total silence to emphasize the dancer's breath and movement.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Early practitioners like Duncan wore loose-fitting tunics and danced barefoot.
Later variants incorporated 'sontuosi' (sumptuous) costumes, ribbons, or spandex.
Lighting and sets are frequently used to enhance the specific mood or concept being interpreted.
on_screen: Image gallery: 1 licensed images with attribution
Reconstruction imagery allowed only from the costume notes, labelled 'reconstruction'

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key figures include Isadora Duncan (founder), Ruth St. Denis (spiritual/Eastern influence), Martha Graham (psychological themes), Doris Humphrey (fall and recovery), and Merce Cunningham (chance procedures).
While originating in the West, the style has adapted 'traditional ethnic movements' into modern expressions.
It is a subclass of dance and a family of modern dance styles.
on_screen: Names on screen as they are spoken
Variant names as a small list

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Interpretive dance is influence of Classical Ballet: Interpretive dance began as a rebellion against its strict rules and restrictive costumes.
Interpretive dance is parent of Modern Dance: Interpretive dance is a family of modern dance styles.
Interpretive dance is sibling of Lyrical Dance: Shares a focus on emotional expression and fluid movement.

tracks.use: chapters: dance it to the music

rules: Original composition only — no sampling, no melody of any existing recording, no lyrics from any song.
Traditional public-domain tunes may be used only when the profile names them and a public-domain source is on file; otherwise compose new material in the idiom.
Keep the proportions true: the meter, the tempo range and the instrument roles the sources describe.
Label every generated track with the tool, the date and this brief, so provenance is always clear.
